title: Ciaran Mulenga Dunne — Principal hearing (2026-07-01)
text:
1

General Pharmaceutical Council
Fitness to Practise Committee
Principal Hearing
Remote videolink hearing
1 – 2 July 2026

Registrant name:
Ciaran Mulenga Dunne
Registration number:

2075118
Part of the register:
Pharmacist
Type of Case:
Caution and misconduct

Committee Members:
Mr Julian Weinberg (Chair)
Fahmina Begum (Lay member)
Thufela Haque (Registrant member)

Secretary:
Chelsea Smith

General Pharmaceutical Council:
Represented by Ms Grace Khaile, Counsel, Case
Presenter

Registrant:
Present and represented by Mr Tim Haines, VHS
Fletchers Solicitors

Facts proved:
N/A
Facts proved by admission:
1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 3 and 4
Facts not proved:
N/A

Fitness to practise:
Impaired by reason of misconduct and caution
Outcome:
9-month suspension order with review
Interim measures:
Interim measure of suspension

2

This decision including any finding of facts, impairment and sanction is an appealable decision
under our rules. Therefore, this decision will not take effect until 31 July 2026 or, if an appeal
is lodged, once that appeal has been concluded. However, the interim suspension set out in
the decision takes effect immediately and will lapse when the decision takes effect or once
any appeal is concluded.

DETERMINATION

Introduction

1.
Mr Ciaran Mulenga Dunne (“the Registrant”), is a Pharmacist first registered with the
General Pharmaceutical Council (“the Council”) on 15 November 2011 under
registration number 2075118.

2.
The hearing is governed by the Pharmacy Order 2010 (“the Order”) and The General
Pharmaceutical Council (Fitness to Practise and Disqualification etc. Rules) Order of
Council 2010 (“the Rules”).

3.
The statutory overarching objectives of these regulatory proceedings are:

“To protect, promote and maintain the health, safety and well-being of the public;
To promote and maintain public confidence in the professions regulated by the
Council; and
To promote and maintain proper professional standards and conduct for members of
those professions.”

4.
The Committee also has regard to the guidance contained in the Council’s “Good
decision making: Fitness to practise hearings and outcomes guidance, revised March
2024” (“the Outcomes Guidance”).

3

5.
This hearing of the Council’s Fitness to Practise Committee (“the Committee”) has
been convened to consider an allegation that the Registrant’s fitness to practise as a
Pharmacist is impaired by reason of his misconduct and by reason of caution.

6.
The Council was represented by Ms Grace Khaile, Counsel. The Registrant has
attended this hearing and is represented by Mr Tim Haines, Solicitor of VHS Fletchers
Solicitors.

7.
The Particulars of the Allegation are as follows:

You, a registered Pharmacist, whilst employed at Well Pharmacy, 11 Market Place,
North Walsham, NR28 9BP (‘the Pharmacy’),

1. On one or more dates between 14 August 2023 - 16 October 2023, took and/or
consumed one or more of the following from the Pharmacy’s stock:
1.1. Aspirin; and/or
1.2. Naproxen; and/or
1.3. Sudafed; and/or
1.4. Diazepam; and/or
1.5. Dioctyl.

2. Your actions in relation to paragraph 1 above were dishonest in that:
2.1
you did not have permission or authority to take and/or consume the
medication from the pharmacy; and/or
2.2
you knew that you were not permitted to take and/or consume the
medication; and/or
2.3
you knew you did not have a valid prescription for Naproxen, Diazepam
and/or Sudafed, which are prescription only items.

3. On or about 20 July 2024, received a caution from Norfolk Police, namely that on or
about 20 September 2023 at North Walsham in the county of Norfolk stole 28 10
mg tablets of Diazepam belonging to the Pharmacy, contrary to section 1 of the
Theft Act 1968.

4

4. Failed to declare the caution in 3 above to the General Pharmaceutical Council
within 7 days as required by Rule 4(2)(b) of the General Pharmaceutical Council
(Fitness to Practise and Disqualification etc. Rules) Order of Council 2010.

By reason of the matters set out above, your fitness to practice is impaired by reason
of your (a) misconduct and (b) caution.

8.
In advance of the hearing, the Committee was provided with a bundle of documentary
material which included, but was not limited to:

•
a statement of case and skeleton argument on behalf of the Council;
•
particulars of the allegation;
•
Copy witness statement of Ms F, Casework Manager at the GPhC dated 15
December 2025;
•
Copy witness statement of Mr B, Professional and Regulatory Standards
Pharmacist at the Well Pharmacy, dated 20 May 2025;
•
Copy witness statement of Mr C, Lead Case Manager, dated 4 June 2025
•
Copy CCTV footage;
•
copy of conditional caution dated 9 November 2024; and
•
the Registrant’s bundle which includes, but is not limited to, his statement, two
reflection statements, a remediation portfolio, a course certificate and overview,
and two character references.

Preliminary applications

Application for part of the hearing to be held in private.

9.
At the outset of the hearing, Mr Haines, on behalf of the Registrant, made an
application that those parts of the hearing that relate to the health and private life of
the Registrant should be held in private. Having invited representations from Ms
Khaile, she agreed that such matters should properly be heard in private.

5

10.
The Committee was aware of the public interest in regulatory hearings being held in
public. This public interest is reflected in Rule 39(1) which provides that “Except as
provided for in this rule, hearings of the Committee must be held in public.” Rule
39(3)(b) provides that the Committee may hold the hearing in whole or in part in
private if it “is satisfied that the interest of the [Registrant] in maintaining their privacy
outweighs the public interest in holding the hearing..…in public.”

11.
Having weighed the Registrant’s right to privacy regarding his health and private life
against the public interest in open justice, the Committee was satisfied that the
Registrant’s right to privacy outweighs the public interest. The Committee was
satisfied that so far as it was intended to refer to the Registrant’s health or private life,
that part of the hearing should be held in private.

Background

12.
The Council relies upon the following witnesses, whose evidence has been agreed, and
who therefore did not attend to give live evidence.

Evidence of Ms F

13.
A witness statement from Ms F who is a case manager with the GPhC, and her
responsibilities include the investigation of fitness to practise allegations and the
preparation of fitness to practise cases for referral to the GPhC committees. Ms F
confirms the obligations a registrant has when convicted of a criminal offence, the
information she received from Lincolnshire Police about the Registrant and what
information the Registrant provided to the GPhC following his criminal conviction.

Evidence of Mr B

14.
Mr B who at the time of providing the statement was employed by Well Pharmacy as a
Professional and Regulatory Standards Pharmacist. Mr B submitted the referral to the
GPhC in respect of the Registrant following an audit at the Pharmacy and following the

6

review of CCTV footage where the Registrant could be seen taking and consuming
pharmacy medication.

Evidence of Mr C

15.
Mr C was employed by the GPhC as a lead case officer. Mr C was allocated the
Registrant’s matter in order to progress the investigation. Mr C further provided
information received from Norfolk Constabulary in relation to the Registrant’s criminal
investigation and subsequent caution.

Registrant’s response

16.
The Registrant provided a bundle in which he admits to all the allegations brought by
the Council. He expressed remorse for his actions towards his previous employer,
colleagues, profession and the public. In his statement dated 25 June 2026, he stated
that:

“I wish to make it clear that I admit to all the allegations brought against me by the
council. I would wish to repeat my sincere apologies for what I have done. Every day I
deeply regret my actions and wish to say sorry to my previous employers, colleagues,
profession, and the Public.”

Findings of facts

17.
The Committee had regard to Rule 28 of the Rules which states:

Rule 28 (Consideration of allegations that relate to more than one category of
impairment) states:
(1) As regards any fitness to practise allegation before the Committee, if—
(a) the particulars of the allegation in the Notice of Hearing relate to more than
one category of impairment of fitness to practise; and
(b) those particulars include a conviction or caution, the chair must ensure (by
adapting the procedure for the hearing, where necessary) that at the principal hearing,
the Committee makes its findings of facts in relation to the allegations that do not

7

relate to the conviction or caution before it hears and makes its findings of fact in
relation to the conviction or caution.

(2) In the circumstances set out in paragraph (1), the chair must also ensure (by
adapting the procedure for the hearing, where necessary), that the Committee only
makes its decision as regards impairment of fitness to practise once it has made its
finding of fact in relation to all the allegations set out in the Notice of Hearing.

18.
The Committee therefore first considered those factual allegations that did not relate
to a caution.

19.
At the outset of the hearing, the Registrant formally admitted all the facts in relation
to allegations 1 (in its entirety), 2 (in its entirety) and 4. The Committee was satisfied
that these admissions amounted to an unequivocal admission and were consistent
with the documentation provided to the Committee. It therefore found the factual
allegations set out in Particulars 1, 2, and 4 proved on the basis of the Registrant’s
admissions, pursuant to Rule 31(6) of the Rules.

20.
In accordance with Rule 28, the Committee then considered those Particulars relating
to the caution. Again, the Committee had regard to the Registrant’s written
statement dated 25 June 2026 in which he confirmed that he attended Grantham
Police Station on 20 July 2024 when a conditional Police caution was administered.

21.
The Committee was therefore satisfied that this admission was unequivocal and was
consistent with the copy of the adult conditional caution provided to the Committee.
It therefore found the factual allegation set out in Particulars 3 proved on the basis of
the Registrant’s admissions, pursuant to Rule 31(6) of the Rules.

Misconduct and Impairment

22.
Article 51(1) of the Pharmacy Order 2010 provides:

“(1) A person's fitness to practise is to be regarded as “impaired” for the purposes of
this Order only by reason of—

8

(a) misconduct;
(j) a police caution in the British Islands;

23.
Rule 5 of the Rules provides:

5(1) The Committee must have regard to the criteria specified in paragraph (2) or,
where appropriate, (3), or, where appropriate, paragraphs (2) and (3), when deciding,
in the case of any Registrant, whether or not the requirements as to fitness to practise
are met in relation to that Registrant.

(2) In relation to evidence about the conduct or behaviour of the Registrant which
might cast doubt on whether the requirements as to fitness to practise are met in
relation to the Registrant, the Committee must have regard to whether or not that
conduct or behaviour—

(a) presents an actual or potential risk to patients or to the public;

(b) has brought, or might bring, the profession of pharmacy into disrepute;

(c) has breached one of the fundamental principles of the profession of pharmacy;
or

(d) shows that the integrity of the Registrant can no longer be relied upon.

24.
Having found all the facts proved, the Committee went on to consider whether the
Registrant’s fitness to practise is impaired by reason of the Registrant’s misconduct
and/or caution.

25.
The Registrant gave evidence. He readily accepted that his actions were dishonest and
that he did not have permission to take the medication in question. He said that on
two occasions, he had stolen diazepam for his own use from the Pharmacy and stated
that, on all but one occasion, the Pharmacy was closed when he took the medication
he had stolen.

9

26.
He stated that at the time, he was experiencing extremely difficult personal
circumstances which left him feeling overwhelmed and unable to cope. However, he
confirmed that he took full responsibility for his actions, and he accepted that his
behaviour fell well below the standard expected of a Pharmacist and breached the
trust that had been placed in him.

27.
He stated that since the incidents in question, he had reflected on his conduct, and
that he felt ashamed, embarrassed and disappointed. He said that he was acutely
aware of the seriousness of his actions and the impact that they had on others.

28.
He said that his difficult personal circumstances resulted in serious lapses in his
professional judgement, which occurred within a difficult emotional context. He
accepted that it did not excuse or justify his actions and that he should have complied
with his professional responsibilities. He accepted that by his conduct, he had
breached Standards 1, 5, 6, 8 and 9 of the applicable standards and that his conduct
resulted in a loss of trust from colleagues, damage to public confidence in him and in
the profession as well as having had a lasting emotional impact on himself.

29.
He stated that since the events in question he had sought professional help and now
recognised the importance of improving his work / life balance and seeking the
support of colleagues. As a result of his more settled personal circumstances, he was
now more level-headed and the circumstances that gave rise to his conduct had now
passed and that he was now in a ‘much better place’. He was not socially isolated and
appreciated the benefit of speaking to colleagues. He accepted that he was now more
proactive in identifying problems and that he was more willing to seek guidance and
support to ensure that he did not become isolated.

30.
He stated that because of these lifestyle changes, he could now manage stress more
effectively and that he now had the ability to reflect on his conduct at times of stress
and could rely on others for support. He stated that he had adopted a healthier
lifestyle and was now better equipped to manage those factors that gave rise to the
conduct that is the subject of this hearing.

10

The Council’s submissions

31.
Regarding the approach to be taken by the Committee at the impairment stage, Ms
Khaile made reference to a number of High Court authorities to assist the way in
which regulatory committees should approach the issue of impairment, including:

• Cheatle v GMC [2009] EWHC 645 (Admin); and
• Roylance and General Medical Council (No.2) [2000] 1 A.C. 311.
• Yeong v GMC [2009] EWHC 1923 (Admin)
• Cohen v GMC [2008] EWHC 581 (Admin);
• Zygmunt v GMC [2008] EWHC 2643 (Admin)
• CHRE v NMC and Grant [2011] EWHC 927 (Admin).

32.
Ms Khaile referred to the case of Cheatle v GMC, in which it said:

“21. There is clear authority that in determining impairment of fitness to practise at
the time of the hearing regard must be had to the way the person has acted or failed
to act in the past. As Sir Anthony Clarke MR put it in Meadow v General Medical
Council [2006] EWCA Civ 1390 [2007] 1 QB 462:

“In short, the purpose of fitness to practise proceedings is not to punish the
practitioner for past misdoings but to protect the public against the acts and omissions
of those who are not fit to practise. The FPP thus looks forward not back. However, in
order to form a view as to the fitness of a person to practice today, it is evident that it
will have to take account of the way in which the person concerned has acted or failed
to act in the past”.

22. In my judgement this means that the context of the doctor’s behaviour must be
examined. In circumstances where there is misconduct at a particular time, the issue
becomes whether that misconduct, in the context of the doctor’s behaviour both
before the misconduct and to the present time, is such as to mean that his or her
fitness to practise is impaired. The doctor’s misconduct at a particular time may be so

11

egregious that, looking forward, a panel is persuaded that the doctor is simply not fit
to practise medicine without restrictions, or maybe not at all. On the other hand, the
doctor’s misconduct may be such that, seen within the context of an otherwise
unblemished record, a Fitness to Practice Panel could conclude that, looking forward,
his or her fitness to practise is not impaired, despite the misconduct”.

33.
Ms Khaile reminded the Committee that the High Court revisited the issue of
impairment in the case of CHRE v NMC and Grant [2011] EWHC 927 (Admin) where
Mrs Justice Cox noted:

“In determining whether a practitioner’s fitness to practise is impaired by reason of
misconduct, the relevant panel should generally consider not only whether the
practitioner continues to present a risk to members of the public in his or her current
role, but also whether the need to uphold professional standards and public confidence
in the profession would be undermined if a finding of impairment were not made in the
particular circumstances.”

34.
Ms Khaile invited the Committee to conclude that the Registrant’s actions breached
the following provisions of the Council’s Standards of conduct, ethics and performance
(2017) (“the 2017 Standards”) and therefore amounted to misconduct.

Standard 5: Pharmacy professionals must use their professional judgement
- Declare any personal or professional interests and manage these professionally
recognise limits of practice.

Standard 6: Pharmacy professionals must behave in a professional manner
- Which means they are trustworthy and act with honesty and integrity.

Standard 9 - Pharmacy professionals must demonstrate leadership
- Do not abuse their position or set out to influence others to abuse theirs.

35.
In relation to current impairment, Ms Khaile submitted that the Committee should pay
careful regard to whether the conduct can be considered easily remediable, whether

12

it has in fact been demonstrably remedied and how this affected the risk of repetition
in the future. In order to assess this, she submitted, the Committee will wish to
explore the Registrant's practice, particularly since the matters of complaint, as well as
the Registrant’s level of insight.

36.
Ms Khaile submitted that, in reaching a decision as to whether the Registrant’s caution
impairs his current fitness to practise, the Committee should take into account the
maintenance of public confidence in the profession and upholding proper standards of
conduct and performance.

37.
She therefore invited the Committee to find that the Registrant’s fitness to practise is
impaired by reason of his misconduct and his caution.

Submissions on behalf of the Registrant

38.
Mr Haines submitted that the individual factors of this case show that the Registrant’s
fitness to practise is no longer impaired and that the public and the profession,
knowing all of the details of this case, would not require a finding of impairment.

39.
He stated that the Registrant was now realistic about returning to a less demanding
role if permitted to return to work, and that he had shown significant insight into his
feelings and recognised the catalyst for those actions that brought him before this
Committee. He reminded the Committee that he now had the support of a mentor
and longstanding friend, Mr. E.

40.
Mr Haines referred to the bundle of documentation including a record of an ethics
course the Registrant had undertaken, as well as a number of positive references.

41.
He stated that bearing in mind the Registrant’s reflections and that the concerns arose
from specific personal circumstances that would not be repeated, the risk of
repetition of any misconduct would be extremely low.

13

42.
He submitted that there was no evidence of actual patient harm being caused and
that the Registrant acknowledged the extent of his dishonesty. He invited the
Committee to have regard to the positive references that have been provided.

43.
He also reminded the Committee that, even if there were no finding of impairment, it
was within its gift under the Article 54(i) to advise or warn the Registrant regarding his
future conduct. He submitted that any advice or warning should set out what went
wrong, why it went wrong, and what the Registrant should do to avoid repeating his
misconduct in the future.

The Committee’s decision on impairment

44.
The Committee has had regard to the submissions made, including the legal
authorities referred to. It has reminded itself that its determination is a matter for its
own independent judgement and that there is no burden or standard of proof that
applies.

45.
The Committee recognises that any failing must be serious such that it would attract a
degree of opprobrium or harsh criticism. The Committee has borne in mind the case of
Spencer v General Osteopathic Council [2012] EWHC 3147 (Admin) and accepts that
“mere negligence does not constitute misconduct” and that “a single negligent act or
omission is less likely to cross the threshold of misconduct than multiple acts or
omissions (The Queen on the Application of Dr Malcolm Noel Calhaem v General
Medical Council [2007] EWHC 2606 (Admin).

46.
Misconduct was defined in the case of Roylance v GMC [2000] 1 AC 311 as, “a word of
general effect, involving some act or omission which falls short of what would be
proper in the circumstances. The standard of propriety may often be found by
reference to the rules and standards ordinarily required to be followed by a medical
practitioner in the particular circumstances”.

47.
The Committee has taken into account all the evidence before it together with both
Ms Khaile’s submissions and those of Mr Haines.

14

48.
It has had regard to Standard 6 of Standards for Pharmacy Professionals which sets
out a fundamental principle of the pharmacy profession with which Pharmacists must
comply. It states that:

“People expect pharmacy professionals to behave professionally. This is essential to
maintaining trust and confidence in pharmacy. Behaving professionally is not limited
to the working day, or face-to-face interactions. The privilege of being a pharmacist or
pharmacy technician, and the importance of maintaining confidence in the
professions, call for appropriate behaviour at all times. There are a number of ways to
meet this standard and below are examples of the attitudes and behaviours expected.”

49.
Noting that there is no evidence of direct harm being caused to any member of the
public by reason of those matters found proved, the Committee was mindful that
Pharmacists are responsible for the safe dispensing of drugs to the public and for
ensuring that only those legitimately entitled to drugs, receive them. As such, the
Registrant, as an experienced Pharmacist, should have had a heightened awareness of
the extent to which his dishonest taking of drugs without a valid prescription might
undermine confidence in the Pharmacy profession.

50.
Additionally, while there was no evidence of actual harm being caused to members of
the public, the Registrant had stolen prescription only medication, including
Diazepam, a controlled drug, whilst at work. The Committee concluded that the
Registrant’s conduct nevertheless posed a risk of patient harm should he have worked
under the influence of such medication.

51.
The Committee was therefore satisfied that the Registrant’s conduct as found proved
in relation to his dishonest use of medication for which he did not have a valid
prescription, represented a serious falling short of the standard expected of a
registered Pharmacist and amounted to serious breaches of Standards 5, 6 and 9. His
conduct had been dishonest, deliberate and repeated over approximately two
months.

15

52.
In reaching its decision, the Committee has borne in mind the following:

• it will be an unusual case where dishonesty is not found to impair fitness to
practise: PSA v HCPC & Ghaffar [2014] EWHC 2723 (Admin);
• dishonesty is almost always extremely serious: Nkomo v. General Medical Council
[2019] EWHC 2625 (Admin);
• findings of dishonesty lie at the top end of the spectrum of misconduct:
Theodoropolous v. General Medical Council [2017] EWHC 1984 (Admin);
• dishonesty encompasses a very wide range of different facts and circumstances,
but that any instance of it is likely to impair a professional person’s fitness to
practise: R (Hassan) v General Optical Council [2013] EWHC 1887;
• the impact on public confidence in cases involving dishonesty, in particular in a
regulatory regime, is not diminished because the practitioner in question is
unlikely to repeat their dishonesty: GMC v Armstrong [2021] EWHC 1658 (Admin);
and
• dishonesty constitutes a breach of a fundamental tenet of the profession GMC v
Igwilo [2016] EWHC 524.

53.
The Committee has also had regard to paragraph 6.8 of the GPhC’s document “Good
decision making: Fitness to practise hearings and outcomes guidance” which states:

“Regulators ensure that public confidence in a profession is maintained. This is a long-
established principle and our standards state that professionals should act with
honesty and integrity to maintain public trust and confidence in the profession. There
are some acts which, while not presenting a direct risk to the public, are so serious they
undermine confidence in the profession as a whole. The GPhC believes that dishonesty
damages public confidence, and undermines the integrity of pharmacy professionals.”

54.
The Committee also considered the Registrant’s failure to declare his caution as
required as found proved in allegation 4. By reason of Rule 4(2)(b) of the Rules,
Registrants are required to declare cautions within seven days. Failure to do so
undermines the Council’s ability to effectively carry out its regulatory role in

16

monitoring the conduct of those on the register, and therefore their suitability to
remain on the register without restriction.

55.
As such, it concluded that the Registrant's conduct in relation to allegations 1, 2 and 4,
both individually and collectively, amounted to misconduct.

56.
In relation to current impairment, the Committee has borne in mind the overarching
objective of fitness to practise proceedings in that it should consider, not only the
need to protect the public, but the need to uphold the reputation of the profession
and to declare and uphold proper standards of conduct and behaviour. In doing so,
the Committee has borne in mind Rule 5(2) of the Rules (which mirror the comments
of Mrs Justice Cox in the case of CHRE v NMC and Grant [2011] EWHC 927 (Admin))
which states:

“In relation to evidence about the conduct or behaviour of the Registrant which might
cast doubt on whether the requirements as to fitness to practise are met in relation to
the Registrant, the Committee must have regard to whether or not that conduct:

(a) presents an actual or potential risk to patients, or to the public;
(b) has brought, or might bring, the profession of pharmacy into disrepute;
(c) has breached one of the fundamental principles of the profession of pharmacy; or,
(d) shows that the integrity of the Registrant can no longer be relied upon.”

57.
The Committee took into account the case of Yeong v GMC [2009] in which it was said:

“It is a corollary of the test to be applied and of the principle that a FTPP is required to
look forward rather than backward that a finding of misconduct in the past does not
necessarily mean that there is impairment of fitness to practise – a point emphasised
in Cohen and Zygmunt…in looking forward the FTPP is required to take account of such
matters as the insight of the practitioner into the source of his misconduct, and any
remedial steps which have been taken and the risk of recurrence of such misconduct. It
is required to have regard to evidence about matter that have arisen since the alleged
misconduct occurred.

17

58.
In the case of Cohen v General Medical Council [2008] EWHC 581 (Admin), it was
noted that when considering the question of impairment, the Committee should give
appropriate weight to the public interest, including the protection of the public, the
maintenance of public confidence in the profession and upholding proper standards of
conduct and behaviour. The Committee is mindful that it is relevant to consider
whether the conduct is easily remediable, whether it has been remedied and whether
it is highly unlikely to be repeated. The Committee notes that the questions posed in
the Cohen case are not a test in which the answers determine the question of
impairment but are a part of the analysing process to be undertaken.

59.
The Committee was satisfied that the Registrant has demonstrated significant insight
into his failings as set out in his written submissions and his oral evidence. However, it
noted that beyond his lifestyle changes, the Registrant has not sufficiently
demonstrated that he now has the practical skills and tools in place to ensure that he
would behave differently if faced with similar stresses in the future, should he have
ready access to medication / drugs.

60.
In relation to the caution administered for theft, the public should quite rightly be able
to expect that Registrants comply with the law. To have failed to do so, the Committee
concluded, undermines confidence in the profession.

61.
In all the circumstances, the Committee concluded that there remained an ongoing
risk that his misconduct and/or criminal behaviour might be repeated.

62.
The Committee has therefore concluded that paragraphs 5(2)(a), (b), (c) and (d) of the
Rules are all applicable in this case. The Registrant had breached a fundamental tenet
of the profession by his criminal and dishonest behaviour. The Committee concluded
that his misconduct and criminal behaviour bring the profession into disrepute.

63.
Furthermore, the Committee determined that a right-minded member of the public,
on hearing all of the circumstances and evidence in this case, including the identified
ongoing public interest concerns, would consider that a finding of current impairment

18

is required if public confidence in the profession and in the regulatory process were to
be maintained. Given the nature and seriousness of the misconduct found proved, and
the identified ongoing risk of harm and to the public interest, the Committee is
satisfied that a finding of impairment is also required to uphold proper professional
standards and that public confidence in the profession which would be undermined if
no such finding were made.

64.
Therefore, the Committee determined that the Registrant’s fitness to practise is
currently impaired on public protection and public interest grounds by reason of his
misconduct and his caution.

Sanction

65.
The Committee, having found that the Registrant’s fitness to practise is impaired,
went on to consider the question of sanction. In doing so, the Committee recognised
that the decision is a matter for its independent judgment.

The Council’s submissions

66.
The Committee heard submissions from Ms Khaile. She referred to her written
skeleton argument regarding how the Committee should approach this stage of the
hearing.

67.
She reminded the Committee to consider whether the Registrant has demonstrated
the requisite level of insight and remorse. She reminded the Committee of the need to
act proportionately to protect the public from the risk of harm and the need to
protect the public interest.

68.
The sanctions available are set out in Article 54(2) of the Pharmacy Order 2010, which
provides that if the Fitness to Practise Committee determines that the fitness to
practise of the person concerned is impaired, it may:

19

• Give a warning to the person and give a direction that the details of the warning
be recorded in the register;
• Give a direction that the entry in the register of the person concerned be subject
to such conditions as the Committee thinks fit to impose for such period not
exceeding three years;
• Give a direction that the entry in the register of the person concerned be
suspended for such period not exceeding 12 months as may be specified in the
direction; or
• Give a direction that the entry in the register of the person concerned be
removed.

69.
Ms Khaile reminded the Committee to have regard to the Outcomes Guidance when
considering a decision on sanction. The Committee should consider sanctions starting
with the least severe and moving up until an appropriate and proportionate sanction
is identified.

70.
Paragraph 6.4 of the Outcomes Guidance states that: “This is not a full list. It is meant
to show that in cases of this type, given the risk to patients and the impact on public
confidence in the profession, removal from the register is likely to be the most
proportionate and most appropriate sanction.”

71.
She submitted that neither giving advice nor a warning is sufficient to deal with the
severity of the misconduct allegations. Conditions are neither workable nor address
the seriousness of the conduct. The Registrant’s conduct was targeted, deliberate and
dishonest. His conduct involved sustained and repeated dishonesty over a period of
time. As such there is a risk of repetition, whilst the Registrant has made admissions
and expressed remorse, he has breached a number of the standards for pharmacy
professionals and failed to exercise professional judgment, honesty and integrity
expected of a pharmacist. The Registrant also breached a number of conditions of the
interim conditions of practice which resulted in the order being replaced with an
interim suspension order. As such, she submitted, the Registrant has shown that he
may not be able to adhere to the restrictions imposed by a Committee to mitigate any

20

risk. She reminded the Committee of the need to protect patients as well as
maintaining public trust and confidence in the profession.

72.
Ms Khaile submitted that the appropriate sanction was a short suspension (suggesting
6 or more months with a review) for the following reasons:

• The Registrant’s dishonest conduct continued over a few months;
• The Registrant had consumed medication whilst at work; and
• He has not demonstrated sufficient remediation.

73.
Such an outcome, Ms Khaile submitted, was an appropriate sanction which
adequately maintained public confidence in the profession and upholds proper
standards of conduct, noting that the Registrant’s conduct, in all the circumstances,
was not fundamentally incompatible with remaining on the register.

The Registrant’s submissions

74.
Mr Haines submitted that there were a number of mitigating factors in this case for
the Committee to take into account, namely:
a) The Registrant has no previous regulatory findings recorded against him;
b) He has been qualified since 2011 and has had an unblemished career;
c) The original incidents that led to the investigations took place nearly 3 years ago;
d) He has admitted to matters during his former employer’s investigation. He
expressed genuine remorse and regret for his behaviour and he cooperated fully
with his former employers in their internal investigation;
e) He cooperated with the police and attending a voluntary interview of which he
made admissions to the specific matters put to him and expressed genuine
remorse and regret for his behaviour;
f) He has cooperated with the regulators throughout the regulatory process;
g) He has made admissions to the Committee at the outset of this hearing;
h) Whilst he has been dishonest, there were mitigating circumstances that led to the
Registrant acting as he did and the circumstances were highly unlikely to arise
again;

21

i) There is no evidence of actual patient harm;
j) The Registrant has been subject to an in interim order since October 2024 and as
such should take into account the principle derived from the case of Kamberova v
NMC [2016] EWHC 2955 (Admin);
k) The Registrant has shown significant understanding and insight by virtue of his
reflections;
l) He has submitted positive character references;
m) He has maintained his professional knowledge; and
n) He has been subject to meaningful counselling.

75.
In relation to the Registrant’s dishonesty, he reminded the Committee of the need to
contextualise the circumstances in which it occurred, noting the Registrant’s
particularly difficult circumstances that was the catalyst for his dishonest behaviour.

76.
Mr Haines submitted that the Committee should take particular account of the fact
that there was no financial gain to the Registrant, that he had been fully cooperative
throughout the internal investigation process, the criminal investigation and the
regulatory process. The Registrant, he submitted, had expressed considerable regret
and remorse and had demonstrated a significant degree of insight.

77.
Mr Haines conceded that, given the Committee’s determination on impairment, that a
warning would not be a realistic outcome, and he also accepted on behalf of the
Registrant, that following a number of breaches, the interim conditions of practice
order had been replaced with an interim suspension order.

78.
He submitted that, if the Committee was minded to impose a sanction of suspension,
then it should be for the shortest meaningful period. In addition, he submitted that it
was open to the Committee to take into account the time spent subject to the interim
suspension order in determining any period of suspension in line with the principle
derived from the case of Kamberova v NMC [2016] EWHC 2955 (Admin).

79.
He further submitted that if a suspension order was imposed, that there was little
purpose in requesting a review, given that, being suspended, the Registrant would be

22

unable to demonstrate compliance with his professional obligations in a pharmacy
setting.

80.
In relation to erasure, Mr Haines submitted that such an outcome was
disproportionate and should be reserved for the most serious cases. He reminded the
Committee of the public interest in keeping an otherwise competent Pharmacist
working to serve the public. Notwithstanding that this was a case of dishonesty, when
properly contextualised, he submitted that the Registrant’s conduct was not
fundamentally incompatible with continued registration.

Committee’s decision on sanction

81.
The Committee has paid due regard to all the evidence received, the submissions
made by Ms Khaile and Mr Haines, and the Outcomes Guidance in considering the
question of sanction.

82.
The Committee recognised the need to act proportionately, in other words that the
sanction should be no more serious than it needs to be to achieve its aims. The
Committee was mindful that the purpose of sanction in regulatory proceedings is not
to punish registrants but is to protect the public and the wider public interest. It was
mindful of the need to weigh the interests of the Registrant against the public
interest, which includes the protection of members of the public, maintenance of
public confidence in the profession, and the declaring and upholding of proper
standards of conduct and performance.

83.
Committee members should use their own judgement when deciding on the sanction
to impose. They should also make sure that any sanction is appropriate and
proportionate, based on the individual facts of the case, and is in the public interest. If
the Committee chooses not to follow the Outcomes Guidance, it should explain why it
has done this in its reasons for choosing the sanction, being mindful that the guidance
represents an authoritative steer.

23

84.
To make sure that the sanction is proportionate, the Committee should consider each
available sanction, starting at the least restrictive, and decide if it is appropriate to the
case. If it is not, the Committee should consider the next sanction, and so on, until it
decides that a particular sanction is appropriate. The Committee should also consider
the sanction immediately above the one it has decided to impose and give reasons
why a more serious sanction is not appropriate and proportionate.

85.
The Committee recognised that in undertaking that task, a sanction may have a
punitive effect. In order to arrive at the right conclusion and to ensure proportionality,
the Committee adopted what is called a ‘stepped’ approach, which involves starting
by considering the least restrictive sanction, and whether that is appropriate, and
continuing until the right and appropriate sanction is reached. The sanction should be
no more severe than is needed to achieve its ends.

86.
The Committee took into account the submissions received, and identified the
following aggravating factors:

• the Registrant’s dishonesty was deliberate and repeated over approximately a two
month period. These factors, the Committee concluded, were of particular
relevance and carried significant weight with the Committee; and
• the theft, which included a controlled drug, related to theft from his employer
which amounted to a significant abuse of trust.

87.
The Committee has identified the following mitigating factors:

• He admitted his dishonest behaviour both during the course of the investigation,
to the Police and at the outset of this hearing;
• He has expressed regret and remorse for his conduct and has demonstrated a high
level of insight;
• He has provided positive references attesting to his clinical competence and
otherwise good character;
• His previous good conduct over a 15 year career; and

24

• The Committee has taken into account his difficult personal circumstances at the
time.

88.
The Committee also gave careful consideration to the Outcomes Guidance. In
particular, the Committee noted the guidance at paragraphs 4.3 and paragraphs 5.17-
5.28 and the section in relation to dishonesty and the duty of candour at paragraphs
6.8-6.14.

89.
The Committee has reminded itself that the outcome of a criminal investigation is not
necessarily a reliable guide to the appropriate sanction to impose bearing in mind the
need within a regulatory context to ensure the maintenance of public confidence in
the profession: R (Low) v General Osteopathic Council [2007] EWHC 2839 (Admin).

90.
It was said in the case of Dey v GMC [2001] UKPC 44:

“The object of disciplinary proceedings against a medical practitioner who has been
convicted of a criminal offence is twofold. It is to protect members of the public who
may come to him as patients and to maintain the high standards and reputation of the
profession. It is not to punish him a second time for the same offence. Nevertheless the
same conduct which constitutes the offence for which he has been convicted may also
demonstrate that the need to maintain the standards and reputation of the profession
or to protect the public or both requires the erasure of his name from the Register.
There is no clear line of demarcation: the difference lies not in the facts themselves but
in the perspective from which they are viewed.”

91.
The Committee was also mindful of the principle derived from the case of Bolton v
Law Society [1991] 1 WLR 512 CA, in which it was said that:

“The reputation of the profession is more important than the fortunes of any individual
member. Membership of a profession brings many benefits, but that is part of the
price.”

25

92.
In considering the sanction appropriate in this case, the Committee first gave
consideration to the aggravating and mitigating features. Having done so, the
Committee first considered taking no action but considered that taking no action
would be insufficient to protect the public or the public interest or to uphold
confidence in the profession given the seriousness and repeated nature of the
Registrant’s dishonesty.

93.
The Committee then considered imposing a warning. Such an outcome may be
appropriate where there is a need to demonstrate to a Registrant, and to the wider
public, that the Registrant’s conduct fell below acceptable standards. Such an
outcome may be appropriate where there is no need to restrict a professional’s right
to practise, there is no continuing risk to the public and where there is need for there
to be a public acknowledgement that the conduct was unacceptable.

94.
However, the Committee considered that the Registrant’s caution and misconduct
related to matters that are significantly too serious for such an outcome. Imposing a
warning, would not adequately address the serious public interest concerns identified.

95.
The Committee next considered whether to impose a period of conditional
registration. The Committee noted that the Outcomes Guidance indicates that
conditions may apply where:

“There is evidence of poor performance, or significant shortcomings in a Registrant’s
practice, but the committee is satisfied that the Registrant may respond positively to
retraining and supervision.
There is not a significant risk posed to the public, and it is safe for the Registrant to
return to practice but with restrictions.”

96.
Given that this case relates to the Registrant’s dishonest behaviour in relation to the
taking of drugs, rather than to clinical shortcomings in his practice as a Pharmacist, the
Committee considered that such a sanction would not be relevant to the facts. This is
not a case in relation to failings in his clinical practice which could be addressed by

26

conditions and in any event, such an outcome was insufficient to mark the seriousness
of the misconduct found proved.

97.
The Committee then went on to consider the imposition of a period of suspension.
The Committee noted from the Outcomes Guidance that suspension may be
appropriate where:

“The committee considers that a warning or conditions are insufficient to deal with any
risk to patient safety or to protect the public, or would undermine public confidence.
When necessary to highlight to the profession and the public that the conduct of the
Registrant is unacceptable and unbefitting a member of the pharmacy profession. Also
when public confidence in the profession demands no lesser outcome.”

98.
Having regard to all the circumstances of this case, the Committee concluded that this
was the appropriate sanction to impose. Such an outcome, it considered, would
reflect the seriousness of the misconduct found proved and send the appropriate
message to the Registrant and the profession generally, that such behaviour is wholly
unacceptable. The Committee considered that a nine-month period of suspension was
the appropriate period of suspension to reflect the deliberate, repeated theft of
medication from his employer, and having balanced all the aggravating and mitigating
factors in this case.

99.
The Committee considered whether removal was appropriate. The Committee noted
the guidance as to when Removal would be an appropriate sanction to impose:

“Removing a professional’s registration is reserved for the most serious conduct. The
committee cannot impose this sanction in cases which relate solely to the
professional’s health. The committee should consider this sanction when the
professional’s behaviour is fundamentally incompatible with being a registered
professional.”

100. Having balanced all the relevant factors identified above, considered that such an
outcome was neither appropriate nor proportionate. The Committee concluded that,

27

subject to being able to satisfy a reviewing committee that the Registrant had taken
further meaningful steps to remediate his dishonest behaviour, there was the
potential for the Registrant to be able to return to practice. To impose a sanction of
removal would therefore be unduly punitive, particularly given the Registrant’s
unusual personal circumstances in which the dishonesty occurred.

101. It therefore determined to impose a suspension order for a period of nine months.
Such a period, the Committee concluded would adequately reflect the serious nature
of the Registrant’s dishonest misconduct and would meet the three limbs of the
overarching objective and yet would give the opportunity to the Registrant to return
to practice subject to further addressing his failings.

Review Hearing

102. The Committee considered that a review hearing was required to ensure that, given
the ongoing risks identified, the Registrant does not return to unrestricted practice
until a review Committee has determined that he has addressed his failings and that
he is fit to do so. A review hearing will be arranged towards the end of the nine-month
period.

103. The Committee considered that any reviewing Committee would be assisted by the
following:

a) any up-to-date reference from his employer or work colleagues, (whether in
relation to voluntary or paid work) which might usefully include particular
reference to the extent to which the Registrant has complied with his obligations
in relation to honesty;
b) any other information the Registrant considers might assist him in returning to
unrestricted practice; and
c) the Registrant’s attendance at a review hearing.

28

Interim Measures

104. The decision to impose suspension of the Registrant’s name from the register will not
take effect until 28 days after the Registrant is formally notified of the outcome, or
until any appeal is concluded.

105. Article 60 of the Pharmacy Order provides that the Committee may order that the
Registrant be suspended with immediate effect if it is satisfied that to do so is
necessary for the protection of members of the public, or is otherwise in the public
interest, or is in the interests of the Registrant.

106. The Committee invited submissions on whether interim measures should be imposed
to cover this period. Ms Khaile invited the Committee to impose an interim measure,
pursuant to Article 60 of the Pharmacy Order 2010, given the rationale for the
Committee’s substantive decision on sanction.

107. Mr Haines submitted that, given that the Committee has imposed a substantive
sanction of suspension, he accepted that the Committee would impose an interim
measure of suspension as not to do so, would permit the Registrant to return to work,
which would be at odds with the Committee’s substantive decision.

108. Given the Committee’s rationale for directing the suspension of the Registrant for nine
months, the Committee therefore concluded that an interim measure was necessary
to protect the public and was otherwise in the public interest in order to maintain
public confidence in the pharmacy profession and the regulatory process. The
Committee concluded that an interim measure of suspension was required for the
same rationale for imposing its substantive sanction of suspension.

109. The Committee therefore imposes an interim measure of suspension on the grounds
that it is necessary for the protection of the public and was otherwise in the public
interest.

110. The current interim order of suspension is revoked.

Decision on Facts

Registrant’s posiƟ on

Decision
29.
The CommiƩ ee accepted the advice of the Legally Qualiﬁed Chair.
30.
The CommiƩ ee took account of the guidance given to the meaning of ‘ﬁtness to
pracƟ se’ in the Council’s publicaƟ on “Good decision-making” (Revised March 2017).
Paragraph 2.11 reads:
“A pharmacy professional is ‘ﬁt to pracƟ se’ when they have the skills,
knowledge, character, behaviour and health needed to work as a
pharmacist…safely and eﬀecƟ vely. In pracƟ cal terms, this means maintaining

31.
In considering whether the Registrant’s ﬁtness to pracƟ se is currently impaired the

the Registrant:
• present an actual or potenƟ al risk to paƟ ents or to the public;
• has brought, or might bring, the profession of pharmacy into disrepute;

The CommiƩ ee also considered whether:

• the conduct which led to the complaint has been addressed

9
• the conduct which led to the complaint is likely to be repeated
• a ﬁnding of impairment is needed to declare and uphold proper standards of

33.
The CommiƩ ee considered that the Registrant’s oﬀences caused harm to all three
colleagues. Colleague C describes feeling anxious, angry, violated, traumaƟ sed and
physically sick. She has subsequently experienced recurring sexual assault dreams as
a result of the Registrant’s behaviour. The other two colleagues were said to be upset

CommiƩ ee considered that this can cause a lack of focus on paƟ ents that could
thereby cause them harm. The CommiƩ ee considers that sexual misconduct of this
nature, intenƟ onally imposing sexual images on colleagues without their consent,
clearly breaches professional boundaries and the relaƟ onship of trust between
colleagues. In one case the vicƟ m was aged only 19 and therefore the Registrant
would have been in a posiƟ on of relaƟ ve power over her as a result. The behaviour
was repeated and was persistent in the face of a clear lack of consent and was

34.
The CommiƩ ee considers that the oﬀences have breached the fundamental

to act professionally and maintain professional boundaries. This type of behaviour

35.
The CommiƩ ee considered that the Registrant’s behaviour breached Standard 6 of

10
Behaving professionally is not limited to the working day, or face-to-face interacƟ ons.
The privilege of being a pharmacist or pharmacy technician, and the importance of
maintaining conﬁdence in the professions, call for appropriate behaviour at all
Ɵ mes.” The CommiƩ ee consider that the oﬀences of this nature are the anƟ thesis of
the professional behaviour expected and the registrant has behaved in a way that

36.
The CommiƩ ee considers that sexual oﬀending of this nature is diﬃcult to remediate.
The CommiƩ ee has no informaƟ on about the compleƟ on of the Registrant’s criminal
sentence. The Registrant has not engaged with the Fitness to PracƟ se proceedings.
The CommiƩ ee has had no evidence of remorse, remediaƟ on, insight or anything

CommiƩ ee ﬁnds that the Registrant has not remediated or addressed his oﬀending
behaviour. The CommiƩ ee therefore considers that there remains a real risk of

and colleagues. The CommiƩ ee considers that a ﬁnding of impairment is necessary

37.
The CommiƩ ee further ﬁnds that a repeƟ Ɵ on of such behaviour would bring the

CommiƩ ee considers that the serious nature of this criminal conduct, that has not

38.
The CommiƩ ee therefore ﬁnds the Registrant’s current ﬁtness to pracƟ se to

Decision on SancƟ on
39.
Having found impairment, the CommiƩ ee has gone on to consider the maƩ er of
sancƟ on. The CommiƩ ee’s powers are set out in ArƟ cle 54(2) of the Order. The
CommiƩ ee should consider the available sancƟ ons in ascending order from least
restricƟ ve, take no acƟ on, to most restricƟ ve, removal from the Register, in order to
idenƟ fy the appropriate and proporƟ onate sancƟ on that meets the circumstances of
the case.
40.
The purpose of the sancƟ on is not to be puniƟ ve, though a sancƟ on may in fact have
a puniƟ ve eﬀect. The purpose of the sancƟ on is to meet the overarching objecƟ ves
of regulaƟ on, namely the protecƟ on of the public, the maintenance of public

11
conﬁdence and to promote professional standards. The CommiƩ ee is therefore
enƟ tled to give greater weight to the public interest over the Registrant’s interests.
41.
The CommiƩ ee had regard to the Council’s Good decision making: Fitness to pracƟ se
hearings and outcomes guidance as revised March 2024 (‘The Guidance’) to inform
its decision.
Council’s Submissions
42.
The CommiƩ ee took into account the submissions made by Mr Hamlet which can be
summarised as follows:
43.
Mr Hamlet conﬁrmed to the CommiƩ ee that the reference on the extract of
convicƟ on to “Sexual Oﬀences Act 2003” cerƟ ﬁcaƟ on was a reference to the fact that
the nature of the convicƟ ons and sentence meant that the Registrant was subject to
noƟ ﬁcaƟ on requirements and would therefore be on the Sex Oﬀenders Register for a
period of 5 years from the date of his convicƟ on.
44.
Mr Hamlet referred the CommiƩ ee to the following secƟ ons of the Guidance:

5.2 - Key factors to consider

5.3 – ProporƟ onality

5.7 – Public interest

5.10 – MiƟ gaƟ ng/AggravaƟ ng factors

5.13-5.14 Circumstances

5.17 – Behaviour and Aƫ
tude

5.19 – Insight and remediaƟ on

6.2-6.7 Sexual Misconduct
45.
Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed that this case had the following aggravaƟ ng factors:

the gravity of the conduct underlying the convicƟ ons

the mulƟ ple vicƟ ms involved

the status of the vicƟ ms as work colleagues

the period over which the conduct occurred

the absence of evidence of any acknowledgement of wrongdoing, insight or
remorse

the absence of evidence of any aƩ empt at remediaƟ on

the risk of repeƟ Ɵ on
46.
Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed there were no miƟ gaƟ ng factors in the case. Mr Hamlet went
on to address the outcomes as outlined in secƟ on 4.3 of the Guidance. He submiƩ ed
that taking no acƟ on and giving a warning were not suitable outcomes given the
seriousness of the oﬀences and the risk to the public that had been idenƟ ﬁed. Mr

12
Hamlet submiƩ ed that condiƟ ons were not appropriate as they would fail to reﬂect
the gravity of the oﬀending and the imposiƟ on of condiƟ ons would not send an

there were pracƟ cal consideraƟ ons relaƟ ng to what condiƟ ons would be workable

47.
Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed that suspension may protect the public and might meet the
gravity of the wrongdoing. However, as a suspension is only for up to 12 months, to

things a suspension order would be bound to fail if no lesser risk would be posed at

48.
Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed that removal was the only appropriate outcome in this case
because the seriousness of the behaviour meant that it was fundamentally
incompaƟ ble with being a registered professional.
Registrant’s posiƟ on
49.
The Registrant had not provided the CommiƩ ee with any evidence or submissions.
The CommiƩ ee noted that his posiƟ on was that he was not to blame.
Decision
50.
The CommiƩ ee accepted the advice of the Legally Qualiﬁed Chair.
51.
The CommiƩ ee ﬁrst considered what, if any, aggravaƟ ng and miƟ gaƟ ng factors there
may be. The CommiƩ ee idenƟ ﬁed the following aggravaƟ ng factors:

Three convicƟ ons which involved three diﬀerent vicƟ ms

Harm was caused to vicƟ ms

Persistent breach of the trust between colleagues

One vicƟ m aged 19

Conduct repeated over 2 years, despite the Registrant being spoken to by an
area manager about his behaviour in 2023

The absence of any evidence of remorse, insight or remediaƟ on
52.
The CommiƩ ee did not idenƟ fy any miƟ gaƟ ng factors on the informaƟ on before it.
53.
The CommiƩ ee went on to consider the available outcomes in ascending order
starƟ ng with the least restricƟ ve. The CommiƩ ee must idenƟ fy the least restricƟ ve
and proporƟ onate outcome that in the parƟ cular circumstances adequately

13
addresses the overarching objecƟ ves of regulaƟ on;  the protecƟ on of the public, the
maintenance of public conﬁdence and the need to promote professional standards.
54.
To take no acƟ on: The Guidance indicates that “This may apply even when
impairment is found, but there is no risk to the public or need to decide on a diﬀerent
outcome.” The CommiƩ ee considered that this outcome would not be appropriate
given the seriousness of the maƩ er and the fact that the CommiƩ ee has idenƟ ﬁed a
risk to the public.
55.
Advice: The Guidance indicates that “Advice can only be given to a professional when
no impairment is found.” The CommiƩ ee therefore found that this outcome was not
available in this case as impairment was found.
56.
Warning:  The Guidance indicates that this outcome may apply when: “There is a
need to demonstrate to a professional, and more widely to the profession and the
public, that the conduct or behaviour fell below acceptable standards. There is no
need to take acƟ on to restrict a professional’s right to pracƟ se, there is no conƟ nuing
risk to paƟ ents or the public, but there needs to be a public acknowledgement that
the conduct was unacceptable.” The CommiƩ ee ﬁnds that this outcome would not
reﬂect the seriousness of the behaviour given that there are criminal convicƟ ons for
sexual oﬀences and the conƟ nuing risk idenƟ ﬁed by the CommiƩ ee.
57.
CondiƟ ons of RegistraƟ on: The Guidance indicates that this outcome may be
appropriate where: “ There is evidence of poor performance, or signiﬁcant
shortcomings in a professional’s pracƟ ce, but the commiƩ ee is saƟ sﬁed that the
professional may respond posiƟ vely to retraining and supervision. There is not a
signiﬁcant risk posed to the public, and it is safe for the professional to return to
pracƟ ce but with restricƟ ons.”
The CommiƩ ee considers that this outcome is not appropriate. There is a signiﬁcant
risk posed to the public and the nature of the risk involving overstepping boundaries
is not one that can be addressed by condiƟ ons and the nature of the behaviour itself
raises issues of compliance. As the Registrant is not engaging, the CommiƩ ee does
not consider that there is evidence there is a willingness or ability to comply with
condiƟ ons and the CommiƩ ee cannot idenƟ fy any workable condiƟ ons. The
CommiƩ ee also considers that the seriousness of the oﬀending and the fact that the
Registrant is on the Sex Oﬀenders Register would mean that condiƟ ons would not
saƟ sfy the public interest.

14
Suspension
58.
The Guidance suggests suspension may be appropriate when:   “The commiƩ ee
considers that a warning or condiƟ ons are not suﬃcient to deal with any risk to
paƟ ent safety or to protect the public, or would undermine public conﬁdence. When it
is necessary to highlight to the profession and the public that the conduct of the
professional is unacceptable and unbeﬁƫ
ng a member of the pharmacy
profession. Also when public conﬁdence in the profession demands no lesser
outcome.”
59.
A suspension would protect the public for the period that it is in force. Under ArƟ cle
54(2) of the Order a CommiƩ ee can impose a suspension for up to 12 months. The
CommiƩ ee notes that the Registrant is on the Sex Oﬀenders Register unƟ l July 2030.
The CommiƩ ee considers that this indicates that a risk to the public will remain for at
least this Ɵ me period. The CommiƩ ee notes that the Registrant has not
demonstrated any remorse remediaƟ on or insight 8 months aŌ er the imposiƟ on of
his criminal sentence, which further suggests that a risk to the public will remain.
Even though orders can be reviewed and extended if a review commiƩ ee considers
that the Registrant remains impaired, the CommiƩ ee do not consider that there is a
likelihood of the Registrant being able to return to safe pracƟ ce aŌ er a period of
suspension.
60.
The CommiƩ ee further considers that conﬁdence in the profession and the regulator
would not be upheld by the imposiƟ on of a 12 month suspension for someone who
has mulƟ ple criminal convicƟ ons for sexual oﬀending against his colleagues and is on
the Sex Oﬀenders Register and has shown no remorse, insight or remediaƟ on.
TreaƟ ng people with dignity and respect goes to the very core of the principles of the
profession and this oﬀending cannot be reconciled with those principles.
Removal
61.
In relaƟ on to removing a pharmacist from the register, the Guidance states:
“Removing a professional’s registraƟ on is reserved for the most serious conduct. The
commiƩ ee cannot choose this outcome in cases which relate solely to the
professional’s health. The commiƩ ee should consider this outcome when the 13
professional’s behaviour is fundamentally incompaƟ ble with being a registered
professional”
62.
The CommiƩ ee has also considered the following paragraphs of the Guidance
relaƟ ng to sexual misconduct at 6.2 -6.5:
“Sexual misconduct – whatever the circumstances – undermines public trust in the
profession and has a signiﬁcant impact on the reputaƟ on of pharmacy professionals.
In some circumstances it can present a signiﬁcant and immediate risk to paƟ ent
safety. It covers a wide range of behaviour, including sexual harassment, sexual

15
assault, physical examinaƟ ons of paƟ ents that are without consent or unnecessary,
and serious sexual oﬀences which lead to criminal convicƟ ons.
The GPhC believes that some acts of sexual misconduct will be incompaƟ ble with
conƟ nued registraƟ on as a pharmacist or pharmacy technician. Removal from the
register is likely to be the most appropriate outcome in these circumstances, unless
there is evidence of clear, miƟ gaƟ ng factors that cause a commiƩ ee to decide that
such an outcome is not appropriate. The misconduct is parƟ cularly serious if:
• there is a convicƟ on for a serious sexual oﬀence
• there is an abuse of the special posiƟ on of trust that a professional has
• it involves a child (including accessing, viewing, or other involvement in images of
child sexual abuse) or a vulnerable adult
• the professional has been required to register as a sex oﬀender or has been
included on a barred list
This is not a full list. It is meant to show that in cases of this type, given the risk to
paƟ ents and the impact on public conﬁdence in the profession, removal from the
register is likely to be the most necessary and proporƟ onate outcome.
The misconduct can take place in many seƫ
ngs. This can be:
• in a private seƫ
ng with family members
• in a social context, or
• in the course of a professional’s work with paƟ ents and colleagues.
It is therefore important that the commiƩ ee carefully considers each case on its
merits, and takes decisions in the light of the parƟ cular circumstances of the case and
the risk posed to paƟ ents and the public….”
63.
The CommiƩ ee considers that the serious nature of the repeated oﬀending and the
fact that the Registrant is on the Sex Oﬀenders Register unƟ l 2030 presents a
substanƟ al ongoing risk of harm to the public and to colleagues that has not been in
any way addressed since the commission of the oﬀences.
64.
The CommiƩ ee considered that there are three convicƟ ons for sexual oﬀences that
resulted in a Community Payback Order and in the Registrant being on the Sex
Oﬀenders Register for 5 years. These oﬀences involved mulƟ ple colleagues, so were
connected to the Registrant’s pracƟ ce, and resulted in a breach of the trust in the
relaƟ onship between colleagues and harm to the vicƟ ms. One of the colleagues was
only 19 years old. The Registrant’s behaviour was persistent, despite a clear
indicaƟ on that the behaviour was unwanted, the Registrant later repeated his
behaviour despite being spoken to by a manager in 2023. He has not demonstrated
any insight, remorse or remediaƟ on. The CommiƩ ee considers that treaƟ ng people
with dignity and respect goes to the very core of the principles of the profession and

16
this oﬀending cannot be reconciled with those principles. The CommiƩ ee considers
that the behaviour is fundamentally incompaƟ ble with being a registered
professional. It is vital to the profession that the public can have conﬁdence and trust
in pharmacists to recognise, respect and uphold principles of dignity and
consent. The Registrant repeatedly demonstrated a persistent disregard for these
principles with his colleagues. The CommiƩ ee therefore considers that only removal
could uphold public conﬁdence in the profession and uphold professional standards.
65.
The Committee considers removal from the register to be the only necessary and
proportionate outcome the circumstances of this case.   The Committee considered
the impact that such an outcome would have on the Registrant but also noted the
case of Bolton v Law Society [1991] 1 WLR 512 CA in which it was said that: “The
reputation of the profession is more important than the fortunes of any individual
member. Membership of a profession brings many benefits, but that is part of the
price.” The Committee has considered principles of proportionality and finds that in
this case the only outcome that would protect the public, uphold proper standards
of behaviour and maintain public confidence in the profession is removal from the
register.
66.
The Committee therefore directs that the Registrar removes Mr Goncalo De Melo
Rodrigues from the Register.
Interim Measure
67.
The ﬁndings of this CommiƩ ee mean that the previous interim order is revoked. The
CommiƩ ee went on to consider interim measures. Interim measures are provided for
under ArƟ cle 60 of the Order and may be imposed aŌ er an order for removal,
suspension or condiƟ ons of registraƟ on. A commiƩ ee can only impose interim
measures if it is saƟ sﬁed that they are needed to protect the public, or are otherwise
in the public interest or in the interests of the professional. Any interim measures will
take eﬀect immediately and can cover the 28-day ‘appeal period’. If the decision is
appealed, the measures will stay in force unƟ l that appeal is decided.
68.
Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed on behalf of the Council that an interim measure of
suspension was required for public protecƟ on and public interest reasons given the
ﬁndings of the CommiƩ ee
69.
The CommiƩ ee did not have any evidence or submissions from the Registrant.
70.
The CommiƩ ee considered that the ongoing risks it has previously idenƟ ﬁed relaƟ ng
to repeated sexual oﬀences against colleagues, the fact that the Registrant is on the
Sex Oﬀenders Register and having not remediated his oﬀences, mean that an interim
suspension measure is necessary for public protecƟ on. The CommiƩ ee considers that
there are immediate risks posed to the public and to colleagues. Further given this

17
posiƟ on and the reasons outlined above, the CommiƩ ee considers public trust and
conﬁdence in the profession, and the regulator would be undermined if the
Registrant was not restricted from pracƟ cing before being removed from the register.
The CommiƩ ee is saƟ sﬁed that it is necessary for an interim measure to be put in
place to protect the public and safeguard the public interest during the appeal
period. The CommiƩ ee is saƟ sﬁed that it is therefore appropriate and proporƟ onate
for an interim suspension to be in place prior to the Registrant being removed from
the register.
71.
The CommiƩ ee hereby orders that the entry of the Registrant in the register be
suspended forthwith, pending the coming into force of the substanƟ ve order.
72.

57.
The evidence in support of this allegation included the audit of the Responsible Pharmacist
(“RP”) record for the relevant period; the audit of what was available from the digital
Controlled Drugs Register for the relevant period together with the Excel spread sheet
demonstrating the supply of controlled drugs made by the Pharmacy during that period; and
the witness evidence of Mr O who was a locum pharmacist working part time at the
Pharmacy.

58.
In relation to sub-particular 1.1, the Committee observed that the audit of the RP record for
the relevant dates showed that there were a number of dates in which there was no entry at
all indicating that an RP was present, although the evidence from Mr L was that the
Pharmacy was opened at least five days a week and also possibly at weekends. Moreover, on
the majority of occasions set out in the audit, where an RP had registered an entry in the
morning, there was no corresponding time entered for when the RP would have terminated
their duty on that day. The Committee noted that this absence of an entry showing the time
of termination applied not only to entries by the Registrant but also those by the witness Mr
O and other RPs.

59.
Whilst the evidence suggested that the RP record had not been kept up to date, there was no
evidence before the Committee of any instances when the Registrant was in fact present as
an RP but had not recorded this. The Committee observed that the Registrant was neither
the Superintendent at the relevant time, (he became the Superintendent later on 14

19

November 2023), nor was he alleged to have been the owner of the Pharmacy. In these
circumstances, the Committee was of the view that the Council had not discharged its
burden to prove that the Registrant had a professional duty to keep the RP record up to date
generally, including in relation to other RPs. Therefore, it could not be said that the
Registrant had “failed” to keep an up-to-date Responsible Pharmacist record.

60.
The Committee noted, in fairness, that Mr Thomas had made what he called a “realistic
concession” in closing submissions on the facts, that the Council’s evidence in support of this
allegation was now somewhat weak.

61.
The Committee found sub-particular 1.1 not proved.

62.
As for sub-particular 1.2, the Committee carefully considered the evidence. Mr Thomas had
submitted that the evidence was from two main sources: Mr L who inspected the Pharmacy
in October 2023; and Mr O who was a locum pharmacist for some of the relevant time.

63.
Mr L had stated in his Investigation Report of 11 October 2023 that the Superintendent had
resigned on 23 September 2023, and the Pharmacy was operating without a nominated
superintendent. His evidence from the inspection was that there was evidence that Schedule
2 controlled drugs were being dispensed and supplied by the Pharmacy but were not entered
into CD registers as was required by law. Staff at the Pharmacy were unsure whether the CD
registers were being kept up to date and it appeared that they thought the Registrant was
responsible for doing so.

64.
The Inspection Report recorded that:

“At the time of inspection, an electronic CD register was in place and entries had been made
for four strengths of Methylphenidate XL. But no other electronic CD records had been made”.

There were also some old paper records dating from April 2021.

99.
Article 54(1) of the Pharmacy Order 2010 provides:

“The Fitness to Practise Committee must determine whether or not the ﬁtness to practise of
the person in respect of whom the allegation is made (referred to in this article as “the person
concerned”) is impaired”.

28

100.
The Council has set out the meaning of ‘ﬁtness to practise’ in its guidance entitled: “Good
decision-making: Fitness to practise Hearings and Outcomes Guidance” (Revised March
2024). Paragraph 2.12 states:
“2.12 A pharmacy professional is ‘ﬁt to practise’ when they have the skills, knowledge,
character, behaviour and health needed to work as a pharmacist or pharmacy technician
safely and eﬀectively. In practical terms, this means maintaining appropriate standards of
competence, demonstrating good character, and also keeping to the principles of good
practice set out in our various standards, guidance and advice.”

101.
Consideration of impairment is undertaken in two stages. First, the Committee has to
consider whether, on the facts found proved, there has been misconduct. It then has to
consider whether, as a result, the Registrant’s ﬁtness to practise is currently impaired. This
approach was outlined by Mr Justice Cranston at paragraph 19 of Cheatle v GMC [2009]
EWHC 645 (Admin):
“A Panel must engage in a 2-step process. First, it must decide whether there has been
misconduct, deficient professional performance or whether the other circumstances set out in the
section are present. Then it must go on to determine whether, as a result, fitness to practise is
impaired. But it may be that despite a [practitioner] having been guilty of misconduct, for
example, a Panel may decide that his or her fitness to practise is not impaired.

145.
Article 54(2) of the Order provides:

“If the Fitness to Practise Committee determines that the person concerned’s ﬁtness to
practise is impaired, it may–

a. give a warning to the person concerned in connection with any matter arising out of or
related to the allegation and give a direction that details of the warning must be
recorded in the person concerned’s entry in the register,
b. give advice to any other person or other body involved in the investigation of the
allegation on any issue arising out of or related to the allegation;
c. give a direction that the person concerned be removed from the register;
d. give a direction that the entry in the Register of the person concerned be suspended,
for such period not exceeding 12 months as may be speciﬁed in the directions; or
e. give a direction that the entry in the Register person of the person concerned be
conditional upon that person complying, during such period not exceeding 3 years as
may be speciﬁed in the direction, with such requirements speciﬁed in the direction as
the Committee thinks ﬁt to impose for the protection of the public or otherwise in the
public interest or in the interest of the person concerned.”

The Committee may also make no order.

outcome may in fact have a punitive eﬀect. The purpose of the outcome is to meet the
overarching objectives of regulation, namely the protection of the public, the maintenance of
public conﬁdence and to promote and uphold professional standards. The Committee is
therefore entitled to give greater weight to the public interest over the Registrant’s interests.
